To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the folding of a protein to its native state is a cooperative process; 2) the native state is a global minimum of free energy and is the only state that is stable at physiological temperatures; 3) proteins with a greater tendency to aggregate have a greater tendency to encrypt an alternative native state; 4) the alternative native state is substantially different in conformation to the monomeric state; and 5) the tendency of proteins to aggregate increases with their instability.

a model of prion disease is presented in which the prion protein can fold into a homodimeric state that is substantially different from its monomeric native structure.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prion protein folding is an example of a more general problem of protein misfolding.

prions are a consequence of the protein folding problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protein folding is not a simple process of a protein finding its lowest energy conformation.
the thermodynamics of protein stability can have important implications in the folding of proteins that are prone to mis-folding.
